newsitem.title: CHINA: FOCUS-S&P move not seen hurting Thai bonds further.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S&P move not seen hurting Thai bonds further.

text.p: Thailand's foreign currency bonds may take in their stride a threat by Standard and Poor's Corp to downgrade the sovereign and key banks because so much bad news already is built into bond prices, analysts said on Friday.
"If you look at spreads in Thailand, they already have factored in the risk of further downgrades," said Chris Francis, head of credit research at Merrill Lynch in Hong Kong.
"It doesn't mean that they won't weaken a bit, but spreads already have weakened signficantly this year," he said.
A Tokyo-based trader agreed.
"I think you will see the bonds marked down initially because of the news, but because it was expected so much, the market will just bounce back and ignore it," he said.
Standard and Poor's Corp said it might cut Thailand's Single-A long-term foreign currency rating and its AA long-term local currency rating.
It also said it might cut the ratings of eight Thai financial institutions.
Traders said the market for Thai bonds has been jittery lately, but not because of fears of further credit downgrades.

Thailand's sovereign Yankee bond due in 2007 reportedly widened out some six basis points in U.S. trade overnight to trade around 94-100 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries on rumours of a coup in Thailand.

Rumours have spread during the past few weeks that Thailand's military was unhappy with the constitution drafting process and with the recent economic crisis in Thailand, but top military officials repeatedly have denied plans of a coup.
S&P said it would review the scale of the country's bad loan problem and financial stress among Thai corporates and prospects for an export-led recovery.

It will also review a government restructuring package to be announced next week and a proposed International Monetary Fund (IMF) economic stabilisation package to help Thailand steady its currency and rescue its banking sector.
"The market is generally comfortable with Thailand over the medium term --the medium term being three to five years," said a fixed-income analyst in Hong Kong.
"It's the one- to two-year horizon and what that may translate into as a result of the IMF stabilisation programme...that has the market a little bit spooked," she said.
In March, Moody's Investors Service downgraded Thailand's foreign currency ceilings for bonds and bank deposits to A3 from A2, citing a deterioration in the country's creditworthiness.
Industrial Finance Corp of Thailand, which on Thursday launched via Lehman Brothers a bond with a credit clause, was one of the banks put on negative credit watch by S&P on Friday.
S&P rates the bank's foreign currency debt at A-minus.
IFCT issued a US$250 million five-year bond at 120 basis points over U.S. Treasuries and a US$250 million 10-year bond, puttable after five years, at 112.5 basis points.
The credit clause stipulates that the issuer must pay an extra 50 basis points if IFCT is downgraded two notches by either S&P or Moody's and another 25 basis points for every downgrade thereafter.
The deal can be put if IFCT's ratings fall below investment grade, which is BBB or higher.
Bankers said the well-received deal was so generously priced that the threat of downgrade may not have much affect on its performance in the secondary market.
In June, IFCT pulled a floating rate note issue shortly after S&P cut its counterparty rating to A-minus, reportedly on fears that it would be forced to offer a wider spread.
That deal paid 41 basis points over the London Interbank Offered Rate for its five year tranche, far less on a swap basis than the fixed-rate bond launched on Thursday.
